answer_text: Mr. Johnson chose the surname "Douglass," suggested by the book "Lady of the Lake," which he had just been reading.

Order, number 3: "Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time." Franklin says this scheme gave him the most trouble: it was practicable for a journeyman printer who controlled his time, but not for a master who had to mix with the world and receive people at their own hours; keeping places for things and papers was also extremely difficult, as he had not been early accustomed to it and his good memory made him less aware of the want of method. He made so little progress, with frequent relapses, that he was almost ready to give up and accept a faulty character in that respect. Even in old age he felt the want of it, and as American Agent in France his lack of business order annoyed colleagues and friends.

Faraday makes the water visible as moisture condensing when the candle burns under a chimney, and shows carbonic acid by pouring lime-water into air collected from the candle, which turns milky.

- In Lecture V, the moisture appearing over the burning candle is identified as water produced from the candle by the action of the air upon its hydrogen [1].
- Also in Lecture V, the other product leaving the chimney is not moisture and is not condensable, so it cannot be shown the same way [1].
- To test for it, clear lime-water is poured into a jar that has collected the air from the candle, and the water becomes quite milky [2].
- Ordinary air does not produce this effect: oxygen, nitrogen, and the other components of common air leave the lime-water perfectly clear [2].
- The milkiness is chalk, formed from the lime of the lime-water combined with something that came from the candle, and it proves to be exactly the same substance as whitening or chalk [6].

Frederick Douglass - model: Master Thomas's copy-books, Webster's Spelling Book Italics, and letters marked on ship timber ("L," "S," etc.) at Durgin and Bailey's ship-yard
Frederick Douglass - practice: writing in spaces left in Master Thomas's copy-book; challenging boys who could write to beat his letters; using a board fence, brick wall, and pavement as copy-book with a lump of chalk as pen and ink
Benjamin Franklin - model: NOT_FOUND
Benjamin Franklin - practice: prose-writing exercises and reading at night after work, before work began in the morning, or on Sundays when alone in the printing-house

Douglass practised by copying letters from copy-books, spelling books, and ship-timber marks using chalk on fences, walls, and pavement, while Franklin practised prose writing in his spare time (nights, early mornings, Sundays) in the printing-house; the evidence does not state what model Franklin used.

Benjamin Franklin - signing indentures: twelve years old
Frederick Douglass - leaving Colonel Lloyd's plantation for Baltimore: between seven and eight years old

Frederick Douglass was younger, at between seven and eight years old, compared with Franklin's twelve.
